posts.title: DuckDB is the analytics database your agent workflows needed
posts.summary: What 14 benchmarks say about wiring agents to DuckDB: 100K inserts in 27 ms, cross-database joins in 8 ms, Parquet a quarter of CSV's size. Plus the DDL shapes that fail loudly.
posts.html:
When you build tools that let an LLM agent query data, the database choice stops being an architecture-slide decision and becomes a failure-mode decision: what happens when the model does something reasonable-sounding but slow, or generates DDL that quietly does not work. I benchmarked that question the slow way — a 14-benchmark suite behind the duckdb-mcp server, measuring everything from DDL speed to MCP round-trip overhead. The numbers argued for DuckDB, and the gotchas were worth the exercise by themselves.

The numbers that changed my defaults

All figures below come from the project's benchmark suite (test_benchmarks.py and the integration tests that pin each practice), run against DuckDB CLI v1.5.4. One machine: 8-core laptop, NVMe, DuckDB 1.5.4 (Variegata) defaults, single run, warm cache. Treat the ratios as the finding and the absolutes as indicative.

Bulk insert: generate_series, never INSERT VALUES. 100,000 users land in 27 ms via a select-from-generate_series. Hand the same task to a model's natural instinct — long INSERT INTO ... VALUES (...), (...) lists — and you are paying parse costs per statement, and the practice guide's rule of thumb is to stop generating them past a thousand rows anyway.

Parquet as the ingest format, not CSV. Parquet files came in around 27% of the equivalent CSV size, and read_parquet queries the file zero-copy without loading it into a database first. For agent pipelines this matters twice: smaller files mean faster handoffs between pipeline stages and cheaper multi-copy retention — files are what agents pass around, after all.

Cross-database joins are instant. Three attached databases of 100K rows each joined in 8 ms. One caveat that cost me an hour: ATTACH needs a path within reach of the session doing the attaching (attached :memory: databases, for what it is worth, do join fine within a single v1.5.4 session), and every CLI invocation is a fresh session — so anything doing cross-process cross-DB work still means temp files, which the server does for you.

Window functions scale flat-ish. ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, running sums and NTILE at 100K rows all landed in a uniform 6.9–7.5 ms band. The kind of analysis an agent is most likely to be asked for is exactly what columnar engines are boringly good at.

JSON output is affordable. The CLI's -json mode adds 9–15% overhead versus plain text. For machine-readable tool responses, that is a tax worth paying — but see the coercion post, because the JSON types need re-hydration.

The failure you will only find at runtime

Here is the one the documentation under-sells: on DuckDB v1.5.4, DEFAULT, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY constraints all work fine. IDENTITY fails with Constraint not implemented!. SERIAL fails earlier, at parse time: v1.5.4 has no SERIAL type at all (Catalog Error: Type with name SERIAL does not exist!). Any model trained on Postgres-heavy corpora will generate SERIAL PRIMARY KEY on demand, all day, and every one of those calls dies.

The fix belongs below the prompt, at the tool level:

CREATE SEQUENCE user_id_seq;
CREATE TABLE users (
  id BIGINT DEFAULT nextval('user_id_seq') PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT UNIQUE CHECK (email LIKE '%@%')
);

Auto-increment through CREATE SEQUENCE + nextval() works and keeps the IDs in the database, where they belong — the practice notes are blunt about it: never generate IDs in Python, use DuckDB-native bulk patterns. Because the MCP server exposes schema creation through recipes that already use the working pattern, the model never gets the chance to discover the failure at 3 a.m. on someone's pipeline.

Why this matters for agents specifically

An agent workflow is an unpredictable query generator with a budget. Three properties of DuckDB line up with that: it is a library-grade database that needs no server to administer (an agent can be handed a file path and be productive immediately), it is columnar and fast on exactly the analytical shapes models tend to write, and its failure modes are loud exceptions rather than silent plan degradations.

The benchmark suite is not an argument that DuckDB beats a warehouse for everything — 500K rows is not big data. It is an argument that for the agent-tooling niche — single-node files, sub-second interactive queries, Parquet in the middle, JSON out the other side — the boring choice is the database that lets your tools encode the three patterns that work (generate_series bulk insert, SEQUENCE auto-increment, Parquet ingest) and make the wrong ones impossible.

posts.title: MCP in production: what the spec doesn't tell you
posts.summary: Field notes from shipping a 15-tool DuckDB MCP server and a six-server orchestrator. The lessons: stdio lifecycle quirks, argument-length walls, JSON type erosion, return-shape chaos, and why direct imports beat JSON-RPC in-process.
posts.html:
The MCP spec is short enough to read in an afternoon and vague enough to hide about a week of debugging in every one of its "implementations MAY" clauses. I shipped two projects that live on both sides of that vagueness: duckdb-mcp, a stdio MCP server exposing 15 DuckDB tools, and orchestrator, a CLI that composes six MCP servers in one process. Here is what the spec did not warn me about.

1. FastMCP gets you a hello world; the low-level server is the job

FastMCP gets you a hello world in ten lines — then hides the three things you need to control. The moment you need a tool router, structured error semantics, or control over the JSON-RPC lifecycle, you want the lower-level mcp.server.stdio API with an explicit Server instance. The DuckDB server ends up as three pieces: a TOOLS list of tool-definition objects with input schemas, a HANDLERS dict mapping tool names to async functions, and a call_tool router that dispatches by name. That separation costs you nothing and pays for itself the first time a tool needs to return a structured error instead of crashing the connection.

2. You will hit the argument-length wall

My first instinct for running SQL through the DuckDB CLI was duckdb -c "SELECT ...". Multi-statement scripts, or anything with bulk data, eventually dies on the OS argument-length limit. The pattern that holds: write the SQL to a temp file and run duckdb -f tmpfile.sql. Same for results: -json mode gives you structured output that you parse yourself. Which leads to the next one.

3. JSON over stdio erodes your types

DuckDB's -json output stringifies more than you would guess, though not uniformly: ints and bools come back as real JSON types, while floats/decimals/dates are strings — SELECT 42 AS i, 1.23::DECIMAL(18,2) AS d returns {"i":42,"d":"1.23"}. Older CLI versions stringified numbers wholesale, so pin the version you test against. If you hand that straight to a model, the model will learn that count looks like "42" and start emitting comparisons against strings. The server has a recursive _coerce_types() pass that walks parsed JSON and converts strings back to int, float, bool, and None. Every tool boundary where you serialize through the weakest format in the pipe needs a re-hydration step on the way back. Nobody tells you this in the protocol docs because the protocol has no types to lose — your data does.

4. Return shapes are folklore, not a standard

When the orchestrator imports six MCP server modules directly (more on that below), I found their call_tool implementations do not agree on anything: one returns a tuple of (list_of_TextContent, dict) where the useful payload lives at index 1; the rest return a bare list of TextContent whose .text is a JSON string. The dispatcher is 15 lines of shape-sniffing. The spec describes what a wire response looks like, not what your in-process handler function returns, so every server you import is a small archaeology dig. Two more discoveries, filed under "why are these not in the README": tool listing lives on the private _tool_manager, not the name you will guess, so plan on reading the SDK source once; and server modules with top-level imports must be imported after sys.path is set up.

5. In-process, skip the wire entirely

JSON-RPC over stdio exists to cross a process boundary. When the consumer is your own Python CLI, that boundary is pure overhead — serialization, subprocess lifecycle, an event loop per server. The orchestrator imports the server modules directly and calls asyncio.run(server.call_tool(name, kwargs)). That collapses "run a code-quality scan, log the findings as tasks, write a wiki report, query the trend in DuckDB" from a distributed-systems problem into one command. The stdio transport stays where it belongs: for external clients like Claude Desktop or IDE integrations.

6. The server is where the lessons belong

duckdb-mcp's most useful feature isn't query execution. It's that nine benchmark-proven practices are encoded in the tools themselves: bulk insert via generate_series instead of INSERT VALUES, CREATE SEQUENCE instead of broken IDENTITY/SERIAL, Parquet-first ingest. The server stops the model from choosing the wrong pattern, which is worth more than any prompt that says "please prefer bulk inserts". Treat your MCP server as the place where operational knowledge becomes a tool constraint.

The spec covers the handshake. Everything above is the part you learn by having the thing fail at 2 a.m., and all of it is now a unit test.

posts.title: Building an eval harness that catches silent model regressions
posts.summary: A deterministic, no-LLM-judge harness for tool-calling reliability that catches the three failure classes an HTTP 200 hides. The first run caught two outright.
posts.html:
Every team that ships an LLM feature eventually builds an eval harness, and every harness eventually answers the same question wrong: did the model succeed, or did the HTTP layer just return 200? This post is the methodology behind the harness I built for local models behind an OpenAI-compatible LiteLLM broker — eight scenarios, three models, two repetitions, and a scoring pass that never asks another model for its opinion.

The scenario suite is fixed and adversarial

The suite ships as eight JSON files. Each scenario defines an OpenAI function schema, a user prompt, simulated tool implementations, and success criteria. The scenarios escalate deliberately:

  • weather_tokyo: one tool call, final answer must cite the tool's value.
  • table_booking: argument extraction. "Eight people" and "7:30 PM" must arrive as party_size: 8 and 19:30.
  • pizza_distractor: an expired coupon in context that must not appear in the call (param_absent).
  • inventory_then_reserve: a two-step dependency. Query the catalog, take the SKU from the tool result, reserve with it.
  • fx_conversion_retry: the first call uses non-ISO currency names and the simulator rejects it; the model must retry with EUR/USD.

The retry scenario is the one that separates models. A single-shot accuracy metric says nothing about whether a model can consume a tool error and recover, which is most of what agent loops actually do.

Deterministic judging, on purpose

There is no LLM-as-judge anywhere in the pipeline. Each emitted tool call is validated against the scenario's function schema: no missing required keys, no extras, no mistyped params. Parameter accuracy is checked under normalization (numbers compared as floats, strings trimmed and case-insensitive). The final answer is graded with criteria like:

{
  "type": "params_exact_any",
  "name": "get_fx_rate",
  "params": { "from_ccy": "EUR", "to_ccy": "USD", "amount": 1200 }
}

(Judge output and results JSON use the key kind for the same concept; scenario files, shown above, use type.)

A fluent-but-wrong answer passes only if it actually states the expected values (answer_contains matches case-insensitively and tolerates thousands separators, so 1,301.04 matches 1301.04). Yes, substring checks are dull. They are also reproducible, which is the property an eval needs when its whole job is telling you that Tuesday's deploy made Thursday worse.

What HTTP 200 hides

Three real findings, all from logging one field deeper than the status code.

Empty content turns. A turn can return 200 with content: null. The harness records empty_content_turns per scenario; a model that "completed" without ever producing usable content now fails loudly instead of silently.

Reasoning burn. One of the tested models is a reasoning model served by vLLM. With a small max_tokens the entire output budget disappears into reasoning_content while content stays null and finish_reason reads length. That combination (finish_reason=length plus empty content plus non-zero reasoning) is scored as a distinct failure mode (reasoning_burn_turns). The shipped run recorded zero burn turns; the metric exists because the failure is cheap to instrument and invisible otherwise. It is also why the reasoning model under test gets max_tokens=2048 on its generation calls while the others run 1024: at 1024, its failure looks like model incompetence when it is really a sampling-budget artifact.

The cache that flattered everyone. The broker response-caches identical request bodies. Sending the same JSON body twice returned the cached completion in ~0.01 s with the same id, which made rep-to-rep variance look near zero and latency look phenomenal. Proof: a repeated body came back in 0.01 s versus ~1.4 s for a distinct one. The fix is one field: every request gets a unique user: mqh-<uuid> stamp to bust the cache. After the fix the same model's per-turn latency showed a real distribution: min 0.83 s, median 1.29 s, max 3.72 s; before the fix it showed a flat line that was never real.

Outages are data, not footnotes

During one re-run, two of the three models were down at the broker: one returned a LiteLLM 404 (the upstream model does not exist), the other a 500 connection error. Both ran anyway and both were recorded as failures with the real HTTP error bodies attached, and the dashboard shows that honestly rather than silently shrinking the comparison to the one live model. Only timeouts and transient codes fail open: 408, 429, and 5xx get the single retry; everything else 4xx (a 404 "model does not exist", a bad request) fails fast with the error body attached. A harness that quietly drops unavailable models is not an eval, it is marketing.

The whole thing is Python 3.13 stdlib only: no pip, no framework, ~5–10 minutes for a full run, and a standalone vanilla-JS dashboard rendered from the results JSON. An eval harness earns its keep on reproducibility, not sophistication: the same input gives you the same number twice, so the day the number moves, you can believe it.

aiCapabilities.html:
A 23-table, ~279M-row ClickHouse database covering Massachusetts government payroll, SBA PPP loans, federal spending, QCEW employment, property values, and IRS income data. The interesting problems are not the queries — they are the coverage traps, the alias-shadowing errors, and the grain mismatches that make naive analysis lie.

What the data covers

The cluster holds 23 tables across ~279M rows spanning six data domains:

Findings

Each finding is traced to its probe dataset (re-runnable SQL with embedded timings in /opt/data/workspace/gov-payroll-workbench/data/).

State payroll (2009–2026)

Latest year (2026): 136,415 employees across 158 departments, total wages $5.59B, average wage $40,994. The 2009 data has only 1 department (partial coverage) vs 155+ in later years — coverage varies significantly across the time series.

Top departments by headcount (latest year): University of Massachusetts System (23,399 employees, $918M wages), MBTA (8,796 employees, $506M wages).

SBA PPP loans (2020–2021)

11.5M loans totaling $797B across 60 states/territories. California leads with 1.27M loans ($104B), Texas second with 939K loans ($63B).

Property values (all years)

1.59M parcels totaling $1.57T in assessed value. Boston leads with 180K parcels ($265B), Cambridge second with 29K parcels ($93B) — Cambridge's per-parcel value ($3.2M) is more than double Boston's ($1.5M).

BLS QCEW employment (2021–2024)

Middlesex County leads with 930K employed and $26.3B in Q4 wages. Suffolk County second with 717K employed and $24.2B in wages.

The coverage traps

Two traps that would make naive analysis lie:

  1. QCEW aggregation levels: the raw table carries 9 aggregation levels per county. Without filtering to agglvl_code = 70 (the county level), employment is overstated ~9x. Diagnosed by noticing the numbers didn't match known county populations.

  2. Federal award modifications: usaspending stores cumulative modifications per award — each amendment adds a new row with the FULL obligated amount, not a delta. Without deduplicating to the final obligation per award_id, spending is overstated ~12x. Diagnosed by cross-checking against published USASpending totals.

The pipeline

The sandbox cannot reach the ClickHouse HTTP port directly. The query layer drives the clickhouse-mcp server over JSON-RPC with SSE responses, handling session-id handshakes, retry with backoff, and stale-session re-handshake. Three real ClickHouse quirks were diagnosed and worked around:

  • Missing arbitrary() aggregate (error 46) — replaced with any()
  • Alias-shadowing ILLEGAL_AGGREGATION (error 184) — CTE restructure
  • fiscal_year stored as string FY2026 — parsed to integer in SQL

The dashboard is a single self-contained HTML file — 51-tile US map, dual-axis SVG trends, and a full SQL provenance section exposing every query, elapsed time, and row count. Opens over file:// with zero network requests.

aiCapabilities.summary: Serve, probe, and benchmark open-weight models across a multi-node GPU cluster — Threadripper Pro head node with dual RTX Pro 6000s, four DGX Spark (GB10) nodes, and an RTX 5090 workstation — through an OpenAI-compatible broker with a failure taxonomy that refuses to call a listed model healthy.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: A heterogeneous GPU cluster — Threadripper Pro head node, dual RTX Pro 6000s, four DGX Spark (GB10) nodes, and an RTX 5090 workstation — serving open-weight models through an OpenAI-compatible broker with probes, benchmarks, and runbooks that keep the fleet honest.
howItWorks: List model groups from GET /models, then health-probe each one — a listed group is not a healthy group.
Classify every failure by latency and response body (engine down vs bad upstream name vs GPU contention) before calling anything dead.
Benchmark sequentially with cache-busting (unique user field plus prompt nonce), logging finish_reason and reasoning burn per turn.
Re-test any surprising throughput claim adversarially (ascending and descending concurrency ladder) before believing it.
Convert persistent DOWN groups into an operator-ready repair runbook instead of narrating failures.

proof.claim: Broker playbook — failure taxonomy, probe scripts, engine forensics
Tested fleet tooling — pulse, bench, runbook generator, 18-test suite
Controlled 50-probe cache experiment proving full-body response caching
Adversarial replay ruling out order-drift in a throughput-collapse claim
Deterministic tool-call scoring harness with dashboard

limits: One large model is resident per GPU at a time; model placement across the cluster is manual, not scheduled.
Engines can only be restarted by the operator — the tooling container has no GPU access and a /v1-only broker allowlist.
Identical request bodies hit the broker cache in ~0.02 s; latency numbers without cache busting are fiction.
GET /models 200 does not mean inference works — probe a chat completion before relying on a group.
aiCapabilities.html: Serving open-weight models across a heterogeneous GPU cluster is the easy part. Knowing what is actually up, how fast, and why something failed is the work.

aiCapabilities.title: Smart routing — RAG, MCP & A2A
aiCapabilities.summary: Making a fleet of MCP servers actually usable: deterministic NL-to-tool planning with guardrails, measured per-tool latency, same-process orchestration, FTS5 retrieval, and agent-to-agent fleet discipline.
aiCapabilities.oneLiner: Guardrail-first tool routing with golden tests, real-latency benchmarks, an in-process MCP orchestrator, FTS5 retrieval, and fleet patterns that survived overnight runs.
howItWorks: Catalog every MCP server's tools with capability classes, then score natural-language goals against name and description signals into a ranked routing table.
Enforce policy before execution — deny-rules veto destructive candidates (duckdb_drop_table is DENIED in read-only mode); plans are dry-runnable.
Replay plans against golden fixtures so routing changes are testable — no LLM in the loop keeps decisions reproducible and auditable.
Measure the fleet with real stdio handshakes — p50/p95 per tool, cold start, error rate — because agent loops hang on the slowest tool.
Compose, don't concatenate — same-process import for zero-overhead calls, FTS5 stores for retrieval, pooled worker fleets for parallel execution.

proof.claim: mcp-router — deterministic NL-to-tool planner with deny-rules and dry-run traces, 13 of 13 golden goals, SHIPPED v0.2.0
mcp-bench — real stdio MCP handshake benchmarks, per-tool p50/p95, cold-start ms, 85 tests
Multi-MCP orchestrator — one CLI over six imported MCP servers, chained pipeline mode
wiki-search — FastMCP server over a SQLite FTS5 search engine
hwdocs RAG store — chunked FTS5 store, 100 percent recall at 0.11 ms vs grep 88 percent at 1.63 ms
Agent-to-agent fleet runner — pooled kanban workers, dispatcher-exact spawn, overnight runbooks

limits: No LLM in the router loop is a feature and a limit — deterministic and golden-testable, but it plans on lexical signals, not semantics.
hwdocs retrieval is lexical FTS5 only; the fleet has an embedding model, but no embedding store is built yet — semantic recall is future work.
Worker fleets cap at about 8 concurrent sessions — a 15-worker dispatcher run crashed the box on RLIMIT_NPROC, documented not folklore.
Kanban workers cannot complete cards under an uncompleted parent umbrella — orchestrators must verify and force-close.
aiCapabilities.html: A fleet of MCP servers is only as good as the layer that routes, measures, and composes it. Guardrails beat scores; golden tests beat vibes.
